findings.finding: There is no opening review of the numerical classifications used directly in the membership, cardinality and complement examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall real-number membership, the impossibility of a negative real square, the even prime, integers and multiples while learning new set notation.
findings.checked: The complete teaching starts with p3-sets and contains no review. The numerical classifications are used directly by the targeted examples. p3-list-elements-a practises even numbers, but does not supply the missing review of real numbers, primes, integers or multiples. No preceding topic or exercise supplies a review.
findings.assumptions: These numerical classifications are prior learning. The review checks recall rather than teaching them. Calculator access does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Add four short items before p3-sets: (1) List the integers from 0 to 6 inclusive and circle the even numbers. (2) List the multiples of 3 from 0 to 12 inclusive. (3) List the primes less than 10 and identify the even prime. (4) Which of −2, 0, 3.5, √5 and √(−3) are real? Can a real number square to −3? Answers: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6, with 0,2,4,6 circled; 0,3,6,9,12; 2,3,5,7, with 2 identified; all except √(−3), and no. Use ordinary lists, without requiring new set notation.

findings.doneWhen: The directly used numerical classifications are rehearsed in a short opening review fitting within one page.

findings.finding: Vary the universal set while holding the selected set fixed to expose how the complement depends on the universe.
findings.breakdown: The existing complement examples do not compare the same selected set across different universal sets.
findings.checked: Each proposed universe contains A, and all proposed complements are correct. Only the universal set changes between successive items. The task uses the complement definition already taught.
findings.assumptions: Complements are taken relative to the stated universal set.

repair.proposal: After p4-complement-question, ask students to predict each change before calculating. Keep A={2,4}. Find A' for (1) U={1,2,3,4}, (2) U={1,2,3,4,5}, (3) U={1,2,3,4,5,6}, (4) U={1,2,4,5,6}. Answers: {1,3}; {1,3,5}; {1,3,5,6}; {1,5,6}. Ask: 'What stayed fixed, what changed, and why did the complement change?' Follow with U={a,b,c,d,e}, B={a,c,e}; find B'. Answer: {b,d}.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict and explain the effect of changing U while A remains fixed, then solve an unpatterned item.

findings.finding: p13-l uses subtraction between sets without defining that operation.
findings.breakdown: Students must interpret (A∪B)−(A∩B) as removal of elements, although preceding teaching defines only membership, cardinality, complements, subsets, intersections and unions.
findings.checked: No earlier teaching defines set difference. p7-demonstrations-o-r models combinations of taught operations, and p13-a-k rehearses those operations. The later cardinality subtraction in p14-addition-rule-block does not define subtraction between sets.
findings.assumptions: Set difference is new within this booklet. Hidden practice solutions are not student-facing teaching.

repair.proposal: Add to p13-l: 'Subtracting a set means removing its elements. Start with A∪B, then remove every element in A∩B.'

findings.doneWhen: The question defines set subtraction before requiring students to shade its result.

findings.finding: Extend the existing comparison to explain the complement of an intersection.
findings.breakdown: Students can reuse the two-diagram comparison to establish the companion relationship between complements and unions.
findings.checked: The identity (A∩B)'=A'∪B' holds for any two subsets of the same universal set, including disjoint and nested sets. The required operations and diagram interpretations are already taught.
findings.assumptions: Both complements use the same universal set.

repair.proposal: After p19-q20-c, offer: 'Shade (A∩B)' on one diagram and A'∪B' on another. What do you notice? Explain why the relationship also holds when the sets are disjoint or one contains the other.' Expected answer: (A∩B)'=A'∪B'. An element outside the intersection is outside at least one of A and B, so belongs to at least one complement.

findings.doneWhen: Students state the identity and explain it using membership, rather than relying only on matching shading.

findings.finding: The introductory card example substitutes event counts without modelling how the descriptions determine them.
findings.breakdown: The intersection count requires selecting even cards strictly less than 20. The solution inserts 9 without showing this decision, leaving the plausible error of including 20 unexposed.
findings.checked: Earlier number-set tasks establish listing and counting, and p21-addition-rule explains subtracting overlap. Neither supplies the particular intersection selection in this example. Independently counting gives 50 even cards, 19 cards below 20 and 9 cards in both events; the resulting probability is 3/5.
findings.assumptions: Students know basic number classifications and counting. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before substitution, add: 'A contains 2,4,…,100, so n(A)=50. B contains 1,2,…,19, so n(B)=19. A∩B contains 2,4,…,18, so n(A∩B)=9. The card numbered 20 is not less than 20.'

findings.doneWhen: The working explicitly identifies the overlap and the origin of each substituted count.

findings.finding: The compound-events topic lacks a review of converting favourable counts into probabilities.
findings.breakdown: Both worked examples divide event counts by the sample-space total as a prerequisite step inside the new compound-event calculation.
findings.checked: All preceding teaching concerns sets, diagrams and cardinalities. The preceding supplied practice, including p19-q20, rehearses set operations rather than count-to-probability conversion. There is no opening review in the compound-events topic.
findings.assumptions: Basic probability is prior learning, consistent with the separate Probability booklets. No calculator is required.

repair.proposal: Before p21-compound-events, add: (1) A bag contains 3 red and 5 blue counters. Select one at random; find P(red). (2) Select one card at random from cards numbered 1 to 10. List the even outcomes and find P(even). (3) Of 20 students, 7 walk to school. Select one at random; find P(walks). Answers: 3/8; 2,4,6,8,10 and 1/2; 7/20.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse identifying favourable outcomes and dividing by the total before the compound-event examples.

findings.finding: Use fixed event probabilities to investigate the possible intersection and union probabilities.
findings.breakdown: The task connects the addition rule to containment and disjointness already represented by Venn diagrams.
findings.checked: For P(A)=3/5 and P(B)=1/4, the intersection ranges from 0 to 1/4. Both extremes are attainable because the marginal probabilities sum to 17/20. The union consequently ranges from 3/5 to 17/20. Only methods available by the end of compound events are needed.
findings.assumptions: Students may construct probability-labelled Venn diagrams rather than enumerate a particular finite sample space.

repair.proposal: After p26-q9, offer: 'Suppose P(A)=3/5 and P(B)=1/4. Find the smallest and largest possible values of P(A∩B). Draw a Venn diagram for each extreme and explain why no smaller or larger value is possible. Hence find the range of P(A∪B).' Expected answer: 0≤P(A∩B)≤1/4, with disjoint events at the minimum and B contained in A at the maximum; 3/5≤P(A∪B)≤17/20.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify both attainable extremes and derive the union range using the addition rule.

findings.finding: The conditional-probability topic lacks a review of multiplying probabilities along a tree path.
findings.breakdown: The multistage investigation and worked example require branch probabilities to be converted into joint probabilities, but the permanent worked tree shows only the resulting numbers.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching does not model path multiplication. p29-teaching-tree identifies conditional branches and joint endpoint events without stating their calculation. The worked tree in p30-diagram-step3 supplies products without operations. Ordinary complementary probabilities are already rehearsed by p21-neither and p22-example-sports, so that component of the candidate is removed.
findings.assumptions: Tree path multiplication is prior learning from Multistage Probability. Calculator access does not remove the need to recall the operation.

repair.proposal: Add a short opening review: 'A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue counters. Select a counter, replace it, then select again. Draw and label the two-stage probability tree. Find the probability of red then blue, writing the operation beside that path.' Expected answer: red branches 3/5 and blue branches 2/5 at each stage; P(red then blue)=(3/5)×(2/5)=6/25.

findings.doneWhen: Students explicitly rehearse path multiplication before encountering conditional branch notation.

findings.finding: Part e has impossible probability data, but the instruction requires a dependent or independent classification in every case.
findings.breakdown: An intersection cannot have probability 0.8 when its containing events have probabilities 0.2 and 0.4. Neither permitted classification describes events satisfying these data.
findings.checked: Independently checking containment gives P(A∩B)≤min(P(A),P(B))=0.2, contradicting 0.8. Earlier classification examples use possible data and supply no validity-check instruction. The hidden answer identifies impossibility, but the student-facing group instruction does not permit that response.
findings.assumptions: The supplied group instruction defines the required responses. Retaining the impossible case preserves its apparent validity-check purpose.

repair.proposal: Change the group instruction to: 'First check whether the probability data are possible. If they are, state whether the events are dependent or independent. If they are impossible, explain why. Remember that P(A∩B) cannot exceed P(A) or P(B).'

findings.doneWhen: Part e can be answered as impossible data, with an explanation, under the student-facing instructions.

findings.finding: Explain the conditions for equal reversed conditional probabilities and test whether that equality implies independence.
findings.breakdown: Students can justify the relationship stated earlier and distinguish equality of reversed conditionals from independence.
findings.checked: With positive marginal probabilities, the conditional formulas show equality exactly when the intersection probability is zero or the marginal probabilities are equal. Both proposed examples are possible and dependent. The formula, equality conditions and independence test are available by the end of the topic.

repair.proposal: After p42-q26, offer: 'Assume P(A)>0 and P(B)>0. Use the conditional probability formula to explain exactly when P(A|B)=P(B|A). Give an overlapping example and a mutually exclusive example. Must such events be independent?' Expected answer: equality holds exactly when P(A)=P(B) or P(A∩B)=0. Marginals 0.4 and 0.4 with intersection 0.2 give both conditionals 0.5 but are dependent because 0.2≠0.16. Mutually exclusive events with marginals 0.2 and 0.3 give both conditionals zero but are dependent because 0≠0.06.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify both equality cases and provide a valid counterexample to the claim that equality implies independence.
